title: The Pit and the Pendulum

teacherSummary.text: Condemned by the Spanish Inquisition in Toledo, the narrator wakes in a pitch-dark cell. He narrowly avoids falling into a central pit, then wakes strapped beneath a razor-edged pendulum descending toward his heart. He smears food on his bonds so rats chew them free. The walls then glow red-hot and close in, forcing him toward the pit, until a French army takes Toledo and General Lasalle catches his arm.

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Down—steadily down it crept” slowly and put it in my own words: The narrator watches the blade come lower and lower, steadily. Next, craft. I notice the dash and the repetition of "down," which make the sentence itself drop in slow steps. The strongest word is “crept”: creeping is slow and sly, and it makes the blade seem alive and patient. Then, effect. How does Poe make the pendulum's movement feel slow? My answer: Poe makes the pendulum's movement feel slow by repeating "down" and stretching the sentence, so we feel every inch; the slowness is the torture, and the suspense comes from waiting, not speed.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the story to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

contentNotes.teacherNote: Sensitive content: Torture; rats. Preview the story, tell students in advance, and allow a pass on reading aloud. Keep discussion on how the writer uses these elements, not on graphic detail. This section mentions drinking or a drug (“…ght. It must have been drugged—for scarcely had I drunk, before I became irresistibly drowsy. A…”). Treat it as period custom or plot detail; name it plainly and don't glamorize it. This lesson mentions suicide or self-harm. Discuss the character's despair and what the text does with it; do not dwell on methods. Before the lesson, remind students that support is available and how to reach the counselor. Check in privately with any student who seems affected and follow your school's referral protocol.
